title: Eight Weeks of Facing What Is Coming
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the fear of what is coming. The Psalms and prophets of trust read in their own setting, not as charms, and a way to live faithfully in an uncertain present.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the person who is afraid of what is coming: for their children, their health, their money, their country, their own death. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It moves slowly on purpose, from naming the fear and what feeds it, down to what lies beneath it, and all along the way it reads the Psalms and prophets of trust where they were first spoken, instead of as charms. It ends with a way of living faithfully in an uncertain present that you can keep when the eight weeks are over.

It is not a cure, and it is not a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the people who know your name. It won't ask you to stop planning, because prudence belongs to faith, and some weeks will ask you to do what is actually yours to do. Walk it at your own pace. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. No one can honestly promise you a safe tomorrow, and these weeks won't try. They point you to the One who is already there.
careNote: If the dread is there most days for weeks, comes as panic, or has turned into hopelessness, see a doctor or a licensed counselor, since caring for your mind is part of trusting God, and in a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.focus: Naming the fear and its true size
weeks.why: Fear of the future rarely stays in one place. It might start with a scan you're waiting on or a rumor of layoffs, then spread to the economy, the country, and the world your children will inherit, and it gets loudest at night when the house is finally quiet. A fear that stays vague can't be answered, only felt. So the first week is simply looking. Written down in plain words, most fears shrink to a size you can pray about, and some to a size you can act on. Look for what is inside them, too. Most fear of the future turns out to be love looking ahead, at people you can't protect from where you stand, and that is a better place to begin than shame.
weeks.practice: Each evening, write down in one plain sentence each thing you're afraid of, as specifically as you can: the test result, the job, the child, the country. Beside each one, write the name of anyone you love who is inside that fear. Don't argue with the list or tidy it up for God. On the last day of the week, circle the one that weighs the most.

weeks.reflection: Which fear on my list weighs the most, and whose face do I see when I think about it?

weeks.focus: The alarm and what feeds it
weeks.why: Your body carries an alarm made for danger in the room, and it can fire at a danger on the other side of the world or twenty years away as if it were at the door. For most of history, news of a distant disaster arrived late or not at all. Now word of catastrophe from anywhere on earth reaches your pocket within minutes, carried by systems built to hold your attention, and few things hold attention like threat. We end up feeling responsible for everything and able to change almost nothing. Many of us, pastors included, read the headlines before we've said a word to God and call it staying informed. Much of the time it is rehearsal. This week is about the order of your inputs: what gets to speak to you first, and what gets the last word before you sleep.
weeks.practice: Put the news on a schedule: one time a day, one or two sources that inform more than they alarm, and a limit you keep. Turn off breaking-news alerts. Keep headlines out of the first hour of your morning and the last hour before sleep, and give the first five minutes of each day to a psalm instead. Psalm 46, which refuses to fear even when the mountains fall into the sea, is a good place to start.

read.label: The News and Fear, on why the feed keeps you afraid and how to set limits

tool.label: The care page for worry that won't switch off, if the alarm keeps ringing after the news is off

weeks.reflection: What reaches my mind first each morning and last each night, and what has it been teaching me to expect from the future?

weeks.focus: A promise first spoken to exiles
weeks.why: Isaiah 41:10 is one of the best-known verses in the Bible, and it's often read as a promise that the thing you dread won't happen. Read the whole chapter. It is addressed to exiles who had already lost their land, their temple, and their king. Around them, frightened nations build idols and nail them down so they won't topple, and those gods are dared to say what is coming, and can't. Ours are quieter, a balance we check for reassurance, a plan with no gaps, a feed that promises we'll see it coming, but they share the same weakness: we have to hold them up. To his frightened people the LORD gives no timetable. He says, “Do not fear, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41:10), and promises to hold them up with his own right hand.
weeks.practice: On the first day, read Isaiah 40 and 41 straight through, noticing who is speaking and to whom. Each day after that, copy Isaiah 41:10 by hand onto a card, then tell God one fear from your list in plain words and say his promise back to him. Keep the card where you will see it at night.

read.label: Isaiah 41 in the Study Bible, with notes on the exiles and the idols that could not tell the future

tool.label: What the Bible Says About Fear and Courage, where the command not to fear comes with a promise of presence

weeks.reflection: What have I been asking God to promise me about tomorrow, and what has he actually promised?

weeks.why: Psalm 91 promises much: no plague near your tent, angels to keep your foot from striking a stone. Many of us learned to pray it like a charm, as if trust were a policy that keeps the bad thing away, and those of us who preach are tempted to teach it that way because frightened people want to hear it. The Gospels show how to hold it. The devil quoted this psalm to Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and dared him to jump. Jesus answered, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7). He would not force a rescue to prove his Father was near. Faith sold as insurance turns every dark possibility into a test of God, and so feeds the fear it promised to cure. The psalm says, “I will be with him in trouble” (Psalm 91:15). It assumes the trouble.
weeks.practice: Each day, pray Psalm 91 aloud for yourself and for the people on your list; it was written to be prayed, and asking God for protection is right. Then add one more sentence in the spirit of the three young men facing the furnace, who told the king their God could rescue them, “But even if He does not,” they would not bow (Daniel 3:17-18). On one of the days, read Matthew 4:1-11.

read.label: Psalm 91 in the Study Bible, including the hard question of why faithful people still fall

tool.label: The Passage Context tool, opened to Matthew 4, where Jesus refuses to test God

weeks.reflection: What proof have I been asking God for, and what would it look like to trust him without it?

weeks.focus: The fear beneath the other fears
weeks.why: Follow almost any fear about the future far enough and it arrives at the one appointment none of us will miss. Hebrews says the Son of God took on our flesh and blood and went into death himself to “free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (Hebrews 2:15). Its first readers had lost property for their faith and stood with those in prison (Hebrews 10:32-34), so the letter knows what danger is. It points them to someone who has gone through death ahead of them and come out the other side. That is why Christian hope rests finally on something that happened, a tomb found empty, which you are free to investigate, rather than on a feeling you have to keep alive.
weeks.practice: Each day, read one of these slowly: Hebrews 2:9-18, John 11:17-27, Romans 8:31-39, 1 Corinthians 15:50-58, Psalm 90. Then tell God plainly what you fear about dying, or about the deaths of the people you love. If there is something you have put off because it means thinking about death, a will, a hard conversation, a letter you have meant to write, begin it this week.

read.label: Facing Death, on the fear of dying and the old Christian art of dying well

tool.label: The Resurrection, a Bible study that weighs the evidence for the event this hope rests on

weeks.reflection: What do I actually believe happens when I die, and how much of my fear about everything else is really fear of that?

weeks.why: Psalm 23 has been read at so many funerals that it can sound like a lullaby, but it bears the name of a shepherd who knew what shepherding cost; David had gone after lions and bears to take back a lamb (1 Samuel 17:34-35). In the psalm, the paths of righteousness in verse 3 run straight into the valley of verse 4, and the shepherd leads his flock through the dark. Notice what happens to the psalm's grammar there. For three verses he speaks about God. In the valley he speaks to him: “for You are with me” (Psalm 23:4). The rod was for predators and the staff for guiding, and both meant the shepherd was within reach. The valley is still walked, but it is walked in company, and some of that company God sends with a human face.
weeks.practice: Each day, pray Psalm 23 slowly, and when you reach verse 4, do what David does and turn from talking about God to talking to him. Before the week ends, tell one person you trust what you've been afraid of. You don't need them to fix it. Ask them to pray for you by name and to check on you again in a few days.

read.label: The Psalms study on honest prayer, whose fourth session walks through Psalm 23

tool.label: Psalm 23 in the Study Bible, with notes on the shepherd's rod and staff

weeks.reflection: Who knows what I'm afraid of, and what would it cost me to let one more person into the valley with me?

weeks.why: Jesus ends his teaching on worry with a realistic line: “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own” (Matthew 6:34). He doesn't pretend tomorrow will be easy. Earlier in the same sermon he taught his disciples to ask for bread one day at a time (Matthew 6:11), the way Israel gathered manna each morning in the wilderness, where the manna hoarded overnight went bad (Exodus 16:19-20). None of this forbids planning. Scripture commends it: “The prudent see danger and take cover” (Proverbs 22:3). Planning makes a decision today about tomorrow and then rests. Worry drags tomorrow's trouble into today, where nothing can be done with it, and carries tomorrow's load with none of tomorrow's grace.
weeks.practice: Each morning, look at your list and ask of each fear whether there is one thing you can do about it today. If there is, do it: make the call, open the mail, book the appointment, update the budget. If there isn't, tell God so and leave it with him until tomorrow. Each night, pray the Lord's Prayer slowly and let the line about daily bread be enough.

read.label: Fear of the Future, on doing today's part and leaving tomorrow's to God

tool.label: The Prayer Generator, with evening prayers and prayers for provision

weeks.reflection: Which of my fears came with something I could actually do this week, and which have I been carrying before their day arrives?

weeks.why: While the exiles waited in Babylon, prophets were promising them a return within two years (Jeremiah 28:3-4). Jeremiah sent a letter that said something harder: “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce” (Jeremiah 29:5). He told them to raise families there, to seek the good of the city where God had sent them, and to pray for it. The exile would last seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10), longer than most who heard the letter would live, and the famous promise of a future and a hope in verse 11 was made to those same people about the far side of that wait. They were told to plant anyway. Fear stops building while it waits to be rescued. Faith puts seed into uncertain ground and trusts God with a harvest it may never see.
weeks.practice: Each day, do one small thing that assumes God will still be there tomorrow: plant something, make plans with a friend, write a letter for a child to open years from now, give to something that will outlast you, pray by name for your town. By the end of the week, write on a card the two or three practices from these eight weeks that actually helped, and keep them.

read.label: The Church Has Been an Exile Before, on Jeremiah's letter and what exiles do on an ordinary Tuesday

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to keep a few of these practices after week eight

weeks.reflection: What have I stopped building while I wait for the fear to pass, and what would it look like to begin it this week?
